items.stem: Define the term 'digital currency'.
items.answer: Money that exists only in electronic form, with no physical notes or coins, and is transferred electronically.

items.stem: Explain why a blockchain is described as decentralised.
items.answer: Copies of the ledger are held by many computers (nodes) in a peer-to-peer network rather than one central authority, and transactions are verified by consensus among nodes.

items.stem: Explain two advantages of electronic funds transfer for a business.

items.answer: A distributed ledger of blocks of transactions; each block includes the previous block's hash; copies on many nodes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Harbour Bank in Cape Town is reviewing its payment methods, including electronic funds transfer and cryptocurrency. Discuss whether Harbour Bank should accept cryptocurrency as a form of payment.

items.answer: A decentralised, distributed ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks, each linked to the previous block by its hash, so records cannot easily be altered.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A decentralised, distributed ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks, each linked to the previous block by its hash, so records cannot easily be altered. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'digital currency' and 'blockchain'.
items.answer: digital currency: Money that exists only in electronic form, with no physical notes or coins, and is transferred electronically. blockchain: A decentralised, distributed ledger in which transactions are grouped into blocks, each linked to the previous block by its hash, so records cannot easily be altered.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: digital currency correctly described; 1 mark: blockchain correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Silverline Couriers, a courier company in Bogotá, is considering accepting cryptocurrency payments from customers. Describe what is meant by a blockchain.
items.answer: A distributed ledger of blocks of transactions; each block includes the previous block's hash; copies on many nodes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Meridian Hospital in Dhaka is reviewing its payment methods, including electronic funds transfer and cryptocurrency. Describe how electronic funds transfer is used to pay staff.
items.answer: Payroll system produces a file of payments; sent to the bank; money moved from the company account to each employee's account on payday.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per step, max 3. [3]

items.stem: Kwame is writing a report for FreshFarm Foods in Doha on how blockchain technology could be used to keep records. Evaluate whether FreshFarm Foods should accept cryptocurrency as a form of payment.
items.answer: Points for: new customers; fast international payments; lower fees; innovative image. Points against / limitations: volatile value; uncertain regulation; low demand; security and accounting issues. Conclusion: it may be worthwhile only if payments are converted immediately to normal currency and demand exists.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: new customers; fast international payments; lower fees; innovative image. Against: volatile value; uncertain regulation; low demand; security and accounting issues. Conclusion may argue: it may be worthwhile only if payments are converted immediately to normal currency and demand exists. [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'confidence (of a rule)'.
items.answer: For a rule "if A then B", the proportion of transactions containing A that also contain B.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: For a rule "if A then B", the proportion of transactions containing A that also contain B. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'data mining' and 'support (of a rule)'.
items.answer: data mining: Searching large amounts of stored data, using software, to discover patterns, trends and relationships that were not previously known. support (of a rule): The proportion of all transactions that contain every item in the rule.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: data mining correctly described; 1 mark: support (of a rule) correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: The security services in Bangkok have asked Meridian Hospital to analyse travel and communication data. Explain why the results of data mining should be checked by experts.
items.answer: Patterns may be coincidental or correlations may not be causes; decisions need human judgement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correlation not causation; 1 mark human judgement. [2]

items.stem: A hospital group run by Meridian Hospital in Auckland wants to use its patient records to improve care. (a) Explain what is meant by data mining. (b) Describe two ways the organisation could use data mining.
items.answer: (a) Analysing large data sets with software to find hidden patterns and relationships. (b) Market-basket analysis; predicting demand; fraud detection; identifying risk factors; customer segmentation; detecting suspicious behaviour.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark large data; 1 mark hidden patterns. [2] (b) 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: MetroBus, a bus company in Seoul, has collected five years of customer transaction data. (a) Explain what is meant by data mining. (b) Describe two ways the organisation could use data mining. (c) Explain one ethical issue with this use of data mining.
items.answer: (a) Analysing large data sets with software to find hidden patterns and relationships. (b) Market-basket analysis; predicting demand; fraud detection; identifying risk factors; customer segmentation; detecting suspicious behaviour. (c) Privacy/consent; profiling individuals; risk of discrimination or false suspicion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark large data; 1 mark hidden patterns. [2] (b) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (c) 1 mark issue; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'gig economy'.
items.answer: A labour market in which people work short-term or task-by-task jobs, often arranged through apps.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A labour market in which people work short-term or task-by-task jobs, often arranged through apps. [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'social networking' and 'gig economy'.
items.answer: social networking: Using websites or apps to create a profile, connect with other people and share content and messages. gig economy: A labour market in which people work short-term or task-by-task jobs, often arranged through apps.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: social networking correctly described; 1 mark: gig economy correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Kwame is researching how IT has changed jobs at Atlas Museum in Karachi over the last twenty years. Describe two ways the organisation could use social networking.
items.answer: Advertising; customer engagement; announcements; recruitment; feedback.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: MetroBus, a bus company in Nairobi, wants to make more use of social media and allow some staff to work from home. (a) Describe two ways the organisation could use social networking. (b) Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of online learning.
items.answer: (a) Advertising; customer engagement; announcements; recruitment; feedback. (b) Flexible time/place; self-paced; recorded; lower costs. Disadvantage: needs devices and internet; less interaction; motivation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark each point, max 3. [3]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'smishing' and 'hacking'.
items.answer: smishing: Phishing carried out using SMS text messages. hacking: Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system, often to steal, change or delete data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: smishing correctly described; 1 mark: hacking correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between 'smishing' and 'two-factor authentication'.
items.answer: smishing: Phishing carried out using SMS text messages. two-factor authentication: A security method that requires two different types of evidence of identity, such as a password and a code sent to a phone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: smishing correctly described; 1 mark: two-factor authentication correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why longer passwords using a mix of character types are harder to crack. (b) Explain how two-factor authentication protects online accounts.
items.answer: (a) The number of possible combinations grows exponentially with length and character set size, so a brute-force attack would take far longer. (b) Even if a criminal learns the password, they also need the second factor (e.g. a code sent to the owner's phone), which they do not have.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark more combinations; 1 mark brute force takes longer. [2] (b) 1 mark two different factors; 1 mark stolen password alone not enough. [2]

items.stem: An attacker can test 100,000,000 passwords per second. Password A has 4 characters chosen from lower-case letters only (26 possible characters); password B has 4 characters chosen from letters, digits and 32 symbols (94 possible characters). Calculate the number of possible passwords for each and the maximum time needed to try them all.
items.answer: A 456,976 combinations, 0.00457 seconds; B 78,074,896 combinations, 0.781 seconds

items.stem: Sunrise Bakery, a bakery in Colombo, suffered a data breach after a hacker gained access to its server. Explain how smishing differs from phishing.
items.answer: Smishing uses SMS text messages rather than email.
items.markingKey: 1 mark text messages; 1 mark otherwise same aim. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Vista Estate Agents in Madrid have received several suspicious emails and text messages this month. (a) Describe three ways users can recognise a phishing message. (b) Explain why staff training is important in preventing these crimes.
items.answer: (a) Generic greeting; urgent/threatening tone; spelling errors; suspicious sender address; links to unusual URLs; requests for passwords. (b) Many attacks rely on tricking people (social engineering), so trained staff are less likely to click links or reveal details.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 3. [3] (b) 1 mark social engineering; 1 mark effect of training. [2]
